activities.title: Series and parallel current/voltage rules with simple circuits
activities.purpose: Establish the current and voltage rules for series and parallel branches and apply them to simple circuits so they can be used in mixed circuits.
activities.instructions: Use only the circuit methods and rules your teacher has taught. In this 25-minute session: (1) Write down the current and voltage rules for series branches and for parallel branches in your own words, with one small example circuit for each. (2) For a simple series circuit with a given voltage and two resistors, find the current through each resistor and the voltage across each resistor, showing every step. (3) For a simple parallel circuit with a given voltage and two resistors, find the voltage across each branch and the current through each branch, showing every step. (4) Check each answer against the rule you wrote: in series the current is the same through all components and the voltages add to the source; in parallel the voltage is the same across all branches and the branch currents add to the source current. If an answer does not match the rule, correct it and explain what went wrong. Do not use advanced methods that have not been taught.
activities.stoppingCondition: Stop when both simple circuits are solved and checked against the rules, or when the 25 minutes are over.
activities.completionCriterion: You have written the series and parallel current/voltage rules, solved one simple series and one simple parallel circuit correctly, and each answer is checked against the matching rule.

activities.title: Changed mixed circuit solve and check
activities.purpose: Show that the series and parallel rules can be combined to solve a mixed circuit and that the result can be checked without help.
activities.instructions: Use only the circuit methods and rules your teacher has taught. (2) Before calculating, write one sentence saying which method or rule you are using and why it applies to this circuit. (3) Solve for the current through and voltage across each component, showing every step. (4) Check your answers against the series and parallel rules: currents in series branches must match, voltages in parallel branches must match, and branch totals must add up correctly. (5) If any answer fails the check, find and correct the error and explain what rule you had applied incorrectly. Do not use advanced methods that have not been taught; if a method is unfamiliar, skip it and use the taught rules instead.

activities.title: Build current/voltage, series and parallel circuit reasoning
activities.purpose: Establish the current/voltage foundation and the series/parallel methods needed before mixed-circuit work.
activities.activityType: Guided conceptual reasoning with worked examples
activities.instructions: Work through the core ideas in this order, writing each step in your own words. 1) Current and voltage: define each, state their units, and explain how a voltmeter and ammeter are connected in a circuit. 2) Series circuits: for two resistors in series, derive and use R_eq = R1 + R2, state that current is the same through all components, and use voltage division V1 = V_total * R1/(R1+R2). Solve one series example with given values. 3) Parallel circuits: for two resistors in parallel, derive and use 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2, state that voltage is the same across parallel branches, and use current division I1 = I_total * R2/(R1+R2). Solve one parallel example with given values. For each example, show the formula, substitute the numbers, and state the final answer with units. If a step is unclear, write down the exact question you would ask your teacher rather than skipping it.
activities.completionCriterion: You have written correct definitions of current and voltage, correct series and parallel rules, and solved one series and one parallel example correctly with units and explained steps.

activities.title: Apply series/parallel methods to mixed circuits and a teacher-style set
activities.purpose: Integrate series and parallel reasoning in mixed circuits and practise under quiz-like conditions.
activities.instructions: 1) Mixed circuits: take one mixed circuit with a series branch and a parallel branch. Reduce it step by step to a single equivalent resistance, then find the total current and the current/voltage in each branch. Show every reduction step. 2) Teacher-style set: without looking at your notes, solve three problems that combine current/voltage, series, parallel and mixed circuits, similar to what a teacher-written quiz would ask. Give yourself about 15 minutes total. 3) After the set, check your answers against your notes or a reliable source. For any wrong answer, correct it and write one sentence explaining the mistake. Do not use advanced methods beyond the series and parallel rules you have already covered.
activities.completionCriterion: You have correctly reduced a mixed circuit, and in the timed set you solved at least two of three problems correctly; any errors are corrected with a one-sentence explanation.

content.activityType: Integrated explanation, guided practice and summary sheet
content.instructions: Use only methods taught in your class. 1) Write the parallel rules: voltage is the same across parallel branches; branch currents add to the total current; branch currents are found from each branch's resistance and voltage. 2) Work through one teacher-style parallel example, finding branch currents and total current. 3) Break a simple mixed circuit into a series part and a parallel part, solve for the current and voltage at each stage, and state which rule you used at each step. 4) Solve one changed mixed circuit with different numbers, checking that the branch currents add to the total and that series voltages add to the source. 5) On one page, write the series and parallel rules and one worked example of each, for review on quiz morning. 6) Note any step you could not do without help; if a step fails, review that specific rule rather than redoing everything.
content.completionCriterion: You correctly solve the changed mixed circuit, show the series/parallel steps and checks, and your one-page sheet contains correct rules and worked examples.

cases.expectation: Capability checks and conceptual/application work; time spent is not mastery.

Work through this in one sitting, writing as you go. Use only the standard Bayes' rule and conditional-probability methods already taught to you; do not assume any advanced methods beyond that repertoire.

1. Write your own one-paragraph explanation of Bayes' rule. In it, explicitly define: the base rate (prevalence) as P(D), the sensitivity as P(+|D), the false-positive rate as P(+|not D), and the posterior P(D|+). State in one sentence how the base rate and sensitivity differ and why swapping them is wrong.

2. Use this changed medical-test example: a disease has prevalence P(D) = 0.02. A test has sensitivity P(+|D) = 0.90 and false-positive rate P(+|not D) = 0.05. A person tests positive. Compute P(D|+).

3. Show every step: write the law of total probability for P(+), substitute the numbers, compute the numerator P(+|D)P(D), compute the denominator, and divide. Keep the base rate and sensitivity in separate labeled lines so the two cannot be confused. Give the final posterior as a decimal and a percentage.

4. Check your answer by a second route: compute P(not D|+) from the same denominator and confirm the two posteriors sum to 1. If they do not, find and correct the actual error before finishing.

5. Write two or three sentences on why you used Bayes' rule here and what would change in the answer if the base rate were much higher while sensitivity stayed the same. Do not claim a general rule that arbitrary parameter changes would not guarantee; state what your specific numbers show.

activities.instructions: Use only the standard Bayes' rule form you have been taught: P(D|+) = P(+|D)P(D) / [P(+|D)P(D) + P(+|no D)P(no D)]. Take a medical-test example with a stated prevalence (base rate) and a stated sensitivity and specificity. Write down: (1) the prior P(D) and explain in one sentence that this is the base rate, not the test's sensitivity; (2) the likelihood P(+|D) and explain that this is the sensitivity; (3) the false-positive term P(+|no D); (4) the total probability of a positive test; (5) the posterior P(D|+). Check each arithmetic step and state the final posterior as a percentage. If any step is unclear, re-derive it from the law of total probability rather than memorizing the formula.
activities.completionCriterion: Your written solution correctly labels prior, likelihood, and posterior, computes the total probability of a positive test, and gives the correct posterior for the worked example; you can state in your own words why the base rate is not the sensitivity.

activities.title: Apply Bayes' rule independently to a changed medical-test example
activities.purpose: Check that you can apply Bayes' rule to an unfamiliar medical-test example without confusing the base rate with sensitivity.
activities.instructions: Without looking back at the worked example, solve a changed medical-test problem with different prevalence, sensitivity, and specificity values. Use the same taught Bayes' rule form. Show: the prior (base rate), the likelihood (sensitivity), the false-positive term, the total probability of a positive test, and the posterior. Then write two or three sentences explaining how the answer would change if the base rate were much lower, and why. If you get stuck, note exactly which quantity you confused and return to the worked example for that step only—do not restart the whole problem unless the confusion is in the setup.
activities.completionCriterion: You independently produce the correct posterior for the changed example, correctly identify the base rate and sensitivity, and give a correct explanation of the base-rate effect.

activities.title: Targeted re-explanation of the confused quantity
activities.purpose: Only if the changed example reveals a remaining base-rate/sensitivity confusion, re-explain that specific distinction with a minimal additional example.

trigger.condition: The changed-example solution mislabels the base rate as sensitivity, omits the prior from the denominator, or produces an incorrect posterior due to that confusion.

activities.instructions: If your changed-example solution confused the base rate with sensitivity or mislabeled the prior, take the specific step where the confusion occurred and re-derive it from the definition: the base rate is P(D) before any test result; sensitivity is P(+|D). Redo only that step on the same changed example and re-check the posterior. Do not redo the entire worked example unless the confusion is in the setup itself.
activities.completionCriterion: You correctly relabel the confused quantity and produce the correct posterior for the changed example.
